group.title: Reasoning and argument
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To admit, often unwillingly, that something is true.
examples: She {conceded} that her plan had flaws.
wrong: He conceded the point by insisting he had been right all along.

words.meaning: To prove that a statement or idea is wrong.
examples: The study {refutes} the old theory.
wrong: The new data refuted the theory by confirming every part of it.

words.meaning: To argue that a claim is false.
examples: The minister {rebutted} the accusations point by point.
wrong: She rebutted the claim by agreeing with it completely.

words.meaning: An argument against another argument.
examples: A good essay deals with the main {counterargument}.
wrong: A counterargument is a point that supports your own view.

words.meaning: A false idea or a flaw in reasoning.
examples: It’s a {fallacy} that bigger is always better.
wrong: A fallacy is a carefully proven truth.

words.meaning: So strong or convincing that you must pay attention.
examples: She made a {compelling} case for change.
wrong: The evidence was compelling, so it convinced nobody.

words.meaning: Having a mistake or weakness.
examples: The research was {flawed} from the start.
wrong: The argument is flawed, so it has no weaknesses.

words.meaning: A conclusion you reach from the information you have.
examples: The {inference} is that sales will keep falling.
wrong: An inference is a fact stated directly in the text.

words.meaning: To reach a conclusion by reasoning from facts.
examples: From the footprints, she {deduced} that two people had been there.
wrong: He deduced the answer by guessing without any facts.

words.meaning: To form an opinion from evidence rather than direct statements.
examples: What can we {infer} from his silence?
wrong: I inferred it because he told me directly and clearly.

words.meaning: To provide evidence that something is true.
examples: Can you {substantiate} that claim?
wrong: He substantiated the claim by offering no evidence at all.

words.meaning: To confirm a statement with more evidence.
examples: Two witnesses {corroborated} her story.
wrong: The second report corroborated the first by contradicting it.

words.meaning: To say the opposite of what someone else said, or to be the opposite of something.
examples: The new figures {contradict} the earlier report.
wrong: The two reports contradict each other because they say the same thing.

words.meaning: To argue that something is not true or correct.
examples: Nobody {disputes} the facts.
wrong: They disputed the result by fully accepting it.

words.meaning: Something you accept as true without proof.
examples: Your {assumption} that he would agree was wrong.
wrong: An assumption is a fact proven by careful tests.

words.meaning: A statement that treats many cases as if they were all the same.
examples: Saying all teenagers are lazy is a {generalization}.
wrong: A generalization describes one single, exact case.

words.meaning: To make something seem more important than it is.
examples: It’s hard to {overstate} the risks.
wrong: He overstated the problem by making it seem tiny.

words.meaning: To think something is smaller, easier or less important than it is.
examples: Never {underestimate} your opponent.
wrong: We underestimated the cost, so it was cheaper than we thought.

words.meaning: Showing small but important differences.
examples: She gave a {nuanced} answer to a hard question.
wrong: His view was nuanced, so it was crude and simple.

words.meaning: Able to be believed or trusted.
examples: The witness was not {credible}.
wrong: The source is credible, so nobody can trust it.

words.meaning: Probably not true, honest or good.
examples: His claims sound {dubious} to me.
wrong: The deal is dubious, so it is clearly honest.

words.meaning: A reason for disagreeing.
examples: Does anyone have an {objection} to the plan?
wrong: My objection is that I fully agree.

words.meaning: A warning that something must be considered.
examples: The offer comes with one {caveat}: it ends tomorrow.
wrong: A caveat is a bonus with no conditions at all.

words.meaning: Something you give up or accept in order to reach agreement.
examples: Both sides made {concessions} to end the strike.
wrong: A concession is refusing to give up anything.

words.meaning: To check that something is true or correct.
examples: Please {verify} your email address.
wrong: I verified the facts by never checking them.

words.meaning: Based on a situation that is imagined, not real.
examples: Let me ask a {hypothetical} question.
wrong: It’s a hypothetical case, so it really happened last week.

words.meaning: Based on guesses, not facts.
examples: The report is purely {speculative}.
wrong: The idea is speculative, so it is based on hard facts.

words.meaning: Based on observation or experiment.
examples: We need {empirical} evidence, not opinions.
wrong: Empirical data comes from opinions, not observation.

words.meaning: Based on personal stories rather than research.
examples: The evidence is only {anecdotal}.
wrong: Anecdotal evidence comes from large, careful studies.

words.meaning: Proving something without any doubt.
examples: There is no {conclusive} proof yet.
wrong: The test was conclusive, so we still have no idea.

words.meaning: Not leading to a clear result.
examples: The results were {inconclusive}.
wrong: The test was inconclusive, so it settled the question completely.

words.meaning: To give reasons for behavior that may not be the real ones.
examples: He {rationalized} his spending as an investment.
wrong: She rationalized her choice by admitting she had no reason.

words.meaning: Careful and detailed examination.
examples: The plan came under close {scrutiny}.
wrong: The report got careful scrutiny, so nobody read it.

words.meaning: To require something to be true already.
examples: Your question {presupposes} that he is guilty.
wrong: Her question presupposes nothing, so it assumes he is guilty.

words.meaning: A weak, false version of an opponent’s argument that is easy to attack.
examples: He attacked a {straw man}, not my real point.
wrong: A straw man is the strongest form of your opponent’s argument.

words.meaning: To change information so that it is no longer accurate or fair.
examples: The small sample {skewed} the results.
wrong: The extra data skewed the results by making them more accurate.

words.meaning: The quality of seeming reasonable or likely.
examples: The story lacks {plausibility}.
wrong: Its plausibility made it impossible to believe.

words.meaning: To prove that something is true or acceptable.
examples: The results were {validated} by a second team.
wrong: They validated the data by proving it was false.

words.meaning: Able to be defended against criticism.
examples: That position is no longer {tenable}.
wrong: The view is tenable, so nobody can defend it.

words.meaning: Not able to be defended.
examples: His argument became {untenable}.
wrong: The claim was untenable, so it was easy to defend.
